title: stele.yaml
description:
The stele manifest: the proto modules this repository owns, the ones it takes from elsewhere, and the code it generates from them.

This schema is not a second description of the format. A test in this repository runs one corpus of example manifests through both this schema and the real parser and fails on any disagreement, so what you read here is what the tool enforces — with the documented exceptions marked "the parser also checks" below, which are rules JSON Schema cannot express.

version.description: Version of the manifest format. Only 1 exists.

modules.description:
The proto modules owned by this repository. Each path is an import root: imports are resolved relative to it.

A manifest is not required to declare one. A repository that owns no protos declares none, and every generate input names a dependency instead.

deps.description:
Proto modules taken from other repositories.

The parser also checks: no two entries may share a name.

generate.description:
The code generation targets.

The parser also checks: no two targets may share a name.

lint.description:
Configuration for `stele lint`.

Absent means every rule at its own default over every file this repository owns — not a lint that does nothing.

The parser also checks: at least one of ignore or rules must be present, and no two rule entries may name the same rule. The lint engine additionally refuses a rule id no loaded rule carries, which this schema cannot express because third-party rules are loaded at run time.

module.title: module
module.description: A proto module owned by this repository.

path.description: Directory of the module, relative to the manifest. It is the import root: a file under it is imported by its path relative to this directory.

dep.title: dependency
dep.description: A proto module taken from another repository.

name.description: Identifies the dependency inside this manifest. A generate input refers to it by this name.

ref.description: The commit SHA to pin to or, for runs that update the lock, a branch or a tag to resolve.

module.description: The module of the producer to take, relative to its repository root. Empty takes the producer's default module.

paths.description:
Narrows what is taken, in coordinates relative to the root of the producer's module. Accepts a single string or a list of strings. Absent takes the whole module.

This decides what the build has, not merely what `export` writes: a file outside the narrowing supplies no import path, is judged by no conflict rule and is named by no drift report. What is narrowed is what is offered, not what is reachable — a file the narrowing excluded is offered again when a file that survived it imports it. A path that selects no file is an error naming what the module does supply.

address.title: git address
address.description:
Where a dependency comes from, in one of three forms:

  https://git.example.com/acme/example.git
  ssh://git@git.example.com/acme/group/example.git
  gh:acme/example            (a shorthand)

The shorthand prefixes are configurable. Two are built in — gh: expands to github.com and glab: to gitlab.com, both over HTTPS — and a caller that configures prefixes replaces those defaults entirely, so a manifest may legitimately use a prefix this schema does not know. The transport is part of the host configuration, not of the shorthand, so the same manifest works from a workstation that clones over SSH and from CI that clones over HTTPS.

There is no git:// form on purpose: it is neither encrypted nor authenticated, and major hosts have disabled it.

The parser also checks: each segment of the repository path must be a real path element, so "." and ".." are refused.

target.title: generate target
target.description: One code generation target: what to generate from, and what to run over it.

name.description: Identifies the target on the command line.

inputs.description: The files to generate from. At least one: a target with no inputs generates from nothing.

plugins.description: The code generators to run over those files. At least one: a target with no plugins produces nothing.

managed.description: Asks for managed-mode file options to be synthesised into the descriptors handed to the plugins. Absent means absent: no options are synthesised at all.

override.description:
The file options to synthesise. At least one — a managed block that overrides nothing reads as if it configured something.

One file option may appear more than once, at most once per path: a repository can put its generated code under more than one import prefix, and a path-scoped override is how that is said. A file matched by several entries takes the LAST of them, so the order here is meaning.

The parser refuses two entries for one option at one path even when their values differ; this schema can only see two entries that are identical in every field, so an editor is quieter here than the tool is.

input.title: input
input.description:
Selects the files one generation request is built from. It names either a local module of this repository or a declared dependency, and exactly one of the two.

The dependency form is not a corner case: a repository that owns no protos generates every line it has from somebody else's. A dependency input takes the module the deps entry already named and does not narrow it further; narrowing within that module is what paths is for.

The parser also checks: module must be a path declared in modules, and dep a name declared in deps.

module.description: The path of a module declared in modules. Mutually exclusive with dep.

dep.description: The name of a dependency declared in deps. Mutually exclusive with module.

paths.description: Narrows the selection, in coordinates relative to the root of the referenced module — this repository's module for module, the producer's module named by the deps entry for dep. Accepts a single string or a list of strings.

oneOf.title: an input from a module of this repository
an input from a declared dependency

plugin.title: plugin
plugin.description:
One code generator invocation.

Where the binary comes from is declared, and there are four ways to declare it, ordered by how much of the answer the manifest gives:

  1. module + version — the tool installs that exact version into its own cache with the Go toolchain and verifies the installed binary's own build metadata against it. Only a Go program can be had this way.
  2. downloads — one entry per platform, each naming a url and the sha256 the download must have. The tool takes the entry matching the machine it runs on, fetches it into its own cache, and verifies the digest before anything is unpacked or run. This is what makes a plugin that is not a Go program genuinely pinnable.

     It is a list, and there is no single-url shorthand, because a digest pins bytes and bytes are per-platform: one url cannot serve linux/amd64 and darwin/arm64. A shorthand would work for whoever wrote the manifest and push the next developer on a different OS back onto an unpinned PATH lookup.
  3. path — an explicit path to a binary, relative to this manifest. It says where the binary is and nothing about which build it is: no version is pinned and none is claimed.
  4. none of the above — the name is looked up on PATH, as it always was. The tool did not choose that binary and does not pretend it did.

Exactly one may be declared. Two would be two answers to a question with one answer.

Half a declaration is refused, and the halves are different mistakes. A version without a module asks for a version of nothing while the tool silently runs whatever PATH holds. A module without a version asks the tool to choose, and any choice it made would be one the manifest does not record. A url without a sha256 is an address, not a pin: whatever the server serves would be run. A download entry without an os and an arch says which bytes to run but not which machine they run on.

The parser also checks: an absolute path is accepted and warned about, because in a committed manifest it resolves on one machine only.

The parser also checks what the schema cannot: that no two download entries claim the same platform, and that a machine no entry covers is refused rather than quietly falling back to PATH.

local.description: The name of, or the path to, an executable plugin binary. It stays the plugin's name whichever tier is declared: it is what the report and the errors call it.

module.description: The Go module path of the command that provides the plugin, as `go install` takes it.

version.description:
The version of module to install. It must be exact — a version `go install` resolves to one build, written out in full, such as v1.36.12. Anything the module system would resolve at run time (latest, upgrade, patch, a branch name, a bare query) puts the manifest back in the business of generating different bytes on different days.

The pattern here checks the shape the parser checks: a leading v, a digit, and at least two dots. It does not check that the version exists, which only `go install` can say.

downloads.description: The published binaries of this plugin, one entry per platform. Exactly one entry may match the machine the tool runs on; two matching entries are refused naming both, and a machine no entry covers is refused naming the platforms that are covered — never a silent fallback to PATH, which is how the un-pinned binary gets back in.

path.description: An explicit path to a binary, interpreted relative to the directory of this manifest — not to the directory the tool was invoked from, which would mean a different binary depending on where it was run.

out.description: The directory the plugin writes to, relative to the manifest.

opt.description: The plugin options, passed through as given. Accepts a single string or a list of strings.

oneOf.title: a plugin the tool installs, at an exact version
a plugin the tool downloads, pinned to a digest per platform
a plugin at a path in this repository

file_option.description: The option to synthesise. The list is short on purpose: an option accepted here but not applied would be a promise the generated bytes do not keep.

path.description: Limits the override to the files under it, in the coordinates an import statement uses. Omitted applies it to every file. It matches on element boundaries and may name a file as well as a directory. Relative, with no leading or trailing slash — the reference tool refuses both spellings too.

stringList.description: A single string or a list of strings. Both forms occur in hand-written manifests, and refusing the scalar would be a gratuitous incompatibility.

download.title: download
download.description:
One published binary of a plugin, for one platform.

os and arch are Go's own spellings — GOOS and GOARCH — because that is what the tool compares them against: runtime.GOOS and runtime.GOARCH, with no translation in between. Accepting a publisher's spelling (x64, macos, aarch64) would need a table nobody can audit, and a table is where a platform gets matched to the wrong bytes while the digest verifies them happily.

os.description: The GOOS the binary is for, spelled as Go spells it.

arch.description: The GOARCH the binary is for, spelled as Go spells it.

url.description: Where this platform's binary, or an archive holding it, is downloaded from. Meaningless without sha256: an address says where the bytes came from, not which bytes they were.

sha256.description: The digest this download must have, as 64 hex characters. It is checked against the bytes as downloaded, before they are unpacked, made executable, run, or admitted to the cache.

archive_path.description:
The member to take when this download is an archive, in the archive's own coordinates. Required when the url names a .tar.gz, .tgz or .zip, and refused otherwise: an archive is not a program, and guessing which of its files is one is a guess the digest cannot protect anyone from.

The parser checks that pairing, which JSON Schema cannot: whether a url names an archive is a fact about the address, not about which fields are present.

lint.title: lint
lint.description: What this repository says about contract linting.

ignore.description:
Import paths no rule is applied to.

Entries are import paths or prefixes of them, matched by whole path components — never globs. `api/legacy/v1/old.proto` names one file; `api/legacy` names everything under it. There is no glob dialect to get subtly wrong, and no question about whether a wildcard crosses a directory separator.

Accepts a single string or a list of strings.

plugins.description:
Rule plugins to load beside the rules this tool ships with. Each serves one or more rules, which are configured under lint.rules by the ids the plugin declares.

The parser also checks: no two plugins may share a name. The host additionally refuses, when the plugins are loaded, a rule that claims the reserved `stele` namespace and two plugins that claim one rule id — neither is expressible here, because both are properties of what the binaries announce at run time rather than of this file.

rules.description:
What this repository says about individual rules. A rule not named here runs at its default severity over every file.

The parser also checks: no two entries may name the same rule.

lint_plugin.title: lint plugin
lint_plugin.description:
One rule plugin: a binary outside this tool that serves lint rules, run beside the built-in ones.

Where the binary comes from is declared on exactly the same terms as a code generation plugin's — the same four tiers, in the same words, with the same refusals, enforced by the same code. See the plugin definition for what each tier means and why half a declaration is refused.

The bare-PATH tier is the one difference from a code generation plugin: it is refused unless the entry also says `unpinned: true`, because the reason the pinning matters here is its own: a rule that is not pinned can change what it says about a repository between two runs of an unchanged manifest, and the first anybody hears of it is a build that reddened overnight.

The rules a plugin serves are named by the plugin itself, and each is configured under lint.rules by that id. Run `stele lint --rules` in this directory for the list, which loads these plugins and prints what they serve.

The parser also checks: no two plugins may share a name, and a name written as a rule id is refused — the plugin is the binary, the rule ids are its to declare.

name.description: The plugin's name in this manifest, and what every error about it says. It is not a rule id: one plugin may serve several rules, and their ids are the plugin's to declare.

module.description: The Go module path of the command that provides the plugin, as `go install` takes it.

version.description:
The version of module to install. It must be exact — a version `go install` resolves to one build, written out in full, such as v1.36.12. Anything the module system would resolve at run time (latest, upgrade, patch, a branch name, a bare query) puts the manifest back in the business of generating different bytes on different days.

The pattern here checks the shape the parser checks: a leading v, a digit, and at least two dots. It does not check that the version exists, which only `go install` can say.

downloads.description: The published binaries of this plugin, one entry per platform. Exactly one entry may match the machine the tool runs on; two matching entries are refused naming both, and a machine no entry covers is refused naming the platforms that are covered — never a silent fallback to PATH, which is how the un-pinned binary gets back in.

path.description: An explicit path to a binary, interpreted relative to the directory of this manifest — not to the directory the tool was invoked from, which would mean a different binary depending on where it was run.

unpinned.description:
Admits that this plugin is whatever the machine's PATH resolves the name to, and is required to declare it that way.

It is the one place a rule plugin is declared on different terms from a code generation plugin. Both answer the same question — which bytes ran — but a generator that answers it with "whatever is on this machine" produces different generated code, which lands in a diff somebody reviews, while a rule that answers it that way produces a different judgement, and a judgement leaves no artefact: the build reddens or greens overnight and nothing in the repository explains it.

So the tier stays spellable and is not usable by accident. Declaring it here is one reviewed line in a file people read, and every report and every `stele lint --rules` listing says the rule is not pinned. It may not be written beside module, downloads or path: those already say where the binary comes from, and the manifest would then be saying two things that cannot both be true.

oneOf.title: a plugin taken from PATH, declared as unpinned
a plugin the tool installs, at an exact version
a plugin the tool downloads, pinned to a digest per platform
a plugin at a path in this repository

lint_rule.title: lint rule
lint_rule.description: What this repository says about one rule.

id.description:
The rule, as `namespace/name`. Rules that ship with this tool live in the reserved `stele` namespace; a third-party rule declares its own. Run `stele lint --rules` for the list that is loaded.

A rule id is a public contract: it appears in this file, so renaming one is a breaking change under the versioning policy. That is why the namespace is here from the first release rather than added at the first collision.

severity.description:
What a finding of this rule costs.

`error` fails the run and is what an unconfigured rule already is. `warning` reports the finding and lets the run pass — this is how a repository adopts lint over contracts that were never linted, in a file a reviewer reads, rather than by adding allow_failure to a CI job nobody looks at. `off` does not run the rule at all.

Note that YAML reads a bare off as false, so it must be quoted.

ignore.description:
Import paths this rule alone is not applied to. Matched exactly as lint.ignore is.

Accepts a single string or a list of strings.
